newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Luxembourg central bank law in trouble - paper.
newsitem.headline: Luxembourg central bank law in trouble - paper.

text.p: A draft law aimed at turning the Luxembourg Monetary Institute (IML) into a fully-fledged central bank in time for European economic and monetary union (EMU) has run into difficulties, newspaper Luxemburger Wort reported.

The newspaper, citing comments made at a conference by the members of parliament responsible for steering the legislation to adoption, said there was a debate in the Grand Duchy about whether the bank should also supervise the financial services industry or whether its functions should be split.

"While the independence of the IML as a central bank is largely accepted, this is not the case for the IML's role as the authority charged with the prudential supervision of the financial services sector where the question of responsibility has another degree of importance," Wort quoted deputy Lucien Weiler as saying.

Weiler said he believed it would be "judicious" to leave supervision ultimately under ministerial authority and that the IML was likely eventually to be composed of two distinct entitities: the central bank in charge of monetary policy and a prudential supervision committee under government control.
The government was presently modifying its draft law "on crucial, if not essential points," Wort quoted him as saying.
Luxembourg's monetary policy is presently exercised by the National Bank of Belgium (NBB) within the two countries' 55-year-old currency union.

The IML was set up in 1983 partly with a view to EMU, but also partly as a response to a 1982 decision by Belgium without consulting Luxembourg to devalue the Belgian and Luxembourg francs by 8.5 percent.

The Grand Duchy must set up an independent central bank under the terms of the Maastricht Treaty on EMU. A draft law doing this was first proposed in 1993 but remained on the government's backburner until late last year.
